arguments.name: Fights are about positions on an unknown line
arguments.conclusion: Every major political fight is an argument about where to sit on a line whose existence and mathematical structure the participants do not know.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: Immigration, guns, abortion, healthcare, criminal justice, climate, AI, culture war, Trump, system rigging, left/right/libertarian disputes are all ongoing fights.
P2: These fights are arguments about where to sit on a line.
P3: Nobody in the argument knows the line exists.
P4: The line has a mathematical structure, a constraint making resolution impossible from inside, a repeating history, and exactly one exit off the line.

st1.quote: This document makes one claim: **they are.**

st2.quote: Every one of those fights is an argument about where to sit on a line.

or1.quote: Every one of those fights is an argument about where to sit on a line.
or1.why: No known prior work frames all political disputes as positions on a hidden mathematical line with a single off-line exit.

or2.quote: It has a history that shows the same pattern repeating across civilizations that never communicated.
or2.why: Offers a claimed cross-civilizational repeating history as new evidence, though no data is given here.

or3.quote: The line has a mathematical structure.
or3.why: Connects political conflict to mathematics and an off-line resolution point, a cross-domain bridge.

or4.quote: It has a constraint that makes resolution impossible from inside.
or4.why: Gestures at a formal constraint but no equation or model is supplied.

arguments.weakest_link: P2, that all these fights are literally arguments about a position on one line, is asserted without argument.
arguments.develop_next: State the line's mathematical structure explicitly and show how each listed fight maps onto a coordinate.

arguments.name: Good and bad are structural properties
arguments.conclusion: Good and bad are structural properties of reality, as invariant as electric charge, not cultural opinions.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The document will show that good and bad are structural properties of reality.
P2: These properties are as invariant as electric charge.
P3: They are not cultural opinions that shift with the century.

st1.quote: That good and bad are structural properties of reality, as invariant as electric charge — not cultural opinions that shift with the century.

st2.quote: That good and bad are structural properties of reality, as invariant as electric charge

arguments.prior_art: Robert Adams, Finite and Infinite Goods (moral realism), 1999

or1.why: Moral realism is old, but the specific invariance-to-physical-charge analogy is a variant.

or2.why: Uses a physics-invariance analogy not standard in moral realist literature.

arguments.weakest_link: P2, the analogy to electric charge invariance, is asserted with no physical or metaethical derivation.
arguments.develop_next: Define the invariance property precisely and give a test that would distinguish it from cultural drift.

arguments.name: No system can determine its own moral direction
arguments.conclusion: No system can determine its own moral direction from inside itself, and this is a proven mathematical result, not philosophy.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The document will show that no system can determine its own moral direction from inside itself.
P2: This is mathematics, not philosophy.
P3: It has been proven.

st1.quote: That no system can determine its own moral direction from inside itself — this is mathematics, not philosophy, and it has been proven.

st2.quote: this is mathematics, not philosophy, and it has been proven

or1.quote: this is mathematics, not philosophy, and it has been proven
or1.why: Reuses the Gödelian self-reference trope applied to morality, a variant rather than a new proof.

or3.why: Applies a formal-limitation result to moral direction, a modest cross-domain move.

arguments.weakest_link: P3, the claim that this has been proven, is unsupported by any cited theorem or derivation.
arguments.develop_next: State the actual theorem and its assumptions, and show the moral-direction case satisfies them.

arguments.name: External reference point must exist
arguments.conclusion: An external reference point must exist for the distinction between good and bad to be meaningful, and such a reference point has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: An external reference point must exist for the good/bad distinction to be meaningful.
P2: Such a reference point has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history.

st1.quote: That an external reference point must exist for the distinction between good and bad to be meaningful — and that such a reference point has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history.

st2.quote: an external reference point must exist for the distinction between good and bad to be meaningful

arguments.prior_art: William Lane Craig, moral argument for God, 1980s

or1.quote: an external reference point must exist for the distinction between good and bad to be meaningful

or2.quote: has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history
or2.why: Adds a historical-record premise the classical moral argument does not use.

or3.quote: has maintained a continuous, accessible record throughout human history
or3.why: Links metaethics to a historical-continuity claim.

arguments.weakest_link: P2, the claim of one continuous accessible historical record, is asserted with no identification of that record.
arguments.develop_next: Identify the record and give criteria for continuity and accessibility across history.

arguments.name: Institutions are captured in ordered sequence
arguments.conclusion: Institutions get captured in a specific, documented, ordered sequence: money first, then government, then education, then reality-interpreters, then moral language itself.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The document will show that institutions get captured in a specific, documented, ordered sequence.
P2: The sequence is money, government, education, reality-interpreters, moral language.

st1.quote: That institutions get captured in a specific, documented, ordered sequence — money first, then government, then education, then the people who interpret reality for everyone else, then the moral language itself.

st2.quote: money first, then government, then education, then the people who interpret reality for everyone else, then the moral language itself

or1.quote: money first, then government, then education, then the people who interpret reality for everyone else, then the moral language itself
or1.why: No known prior work specifies this exact ordered capture sequence.

or2.why: Claims documentation as new evidence, though none is exhibited here.

or3.why: Extends institutional-capture theory into moral language, a cross-domain move.

arguments.weakest_link: P1, that the sequence is documented, is asserted without any documentation.
arguments.develop_next: Provide dated case studies showing each stage preceding the next across multiple societies.

arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The enforcement mechanism is shame, not force.
P2: Governments have been deploying shame as official policy since at least 2015.

st1.quote: That the enforcement mechanism is not force but shame — and that governments have been deploying it as official policy since at least 2015.

st2.quote: the enforcement mechanism is not force but shame

or2.quote: governments have been deploying it as official policy since at least 2015
or2.why: Offers a dated policy claim as new evidence, though uncited here.

or3.quote: the enforcement mechanism is not force but shame

arguments.weakest_link: P2, the dated claim that governments have deployed shame as official policy since 2015, is unsupported.

arguments.name: Population sorts by connection to truth
arguments.conclusion: The population sorts into two classes over time, defined not by demographics but by whether their connection to truth runs through captured institutions or directly to the source.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe
premises: P1: The population sorts into two classes over time.
P2: The sorting is defined by one structural feature: connection to truth via captured institutions or directly to the source.
P3: It is not defined by any demographic variable.

st1.quote: That the population sorts into two classes over time, defined not by any demographic variable but by one structural feature: whether their connection to truth runs through the captured institutions or directly to the source.

st2.quote: defined not by any demographic variable but by one structural feature: whether their connection to truth runs through the captured institutions or directly to the source

or1.quote: defined not by any demographic variable but by one structural feature: whether their connection to truth runs through the captured institutions or directly to the source

or3.quote: connection to truth runs through the captured institutions or directly to the source

arguments.name: Communication technologies follow capture pattern
arguments.conclusion: Every communication technology in history follows the same pattern: a brief window where truth spreads, followed by institutional capture of the infrastructure.
arguments.speaker: David Lowe

P2: Each follows the same pattern: brief truth-spread window, then institutional capture of infrastructure.

st1.quote: That every communication technology in history — writing, the printing press, radio, television, the internet, social media — follows the same pattern: a brief window where truth spreads, followed by institutional capture of the infrastructure.

P2: It shows justice and mercy cannot both be fully satisfied inside any closed system.
P3: Someone always eats the deficit.
